objective_for_doctor: Assess and diagnose the patient presenting with rectal bleeding and a palpable rectal mass.

turns.content: Doctor: I’m Dr. Agent—I'll ask a few quick questions. 1) How old are you, and is the rectal bleeding bright red (on toilet paper) or darker/maroon? Doctor: 2) How long has the bleeding and rectal mass been present, and do you feel weight loss, change in bowel habits, or pain?
Patient: I’m 45, and the bleeding is bright red on toilet paper. It’s been going on for about two weeks, and I haven’t had weight loss, any change in bowel habits, or any pain with bowel movements.

Doctor: Thanks—bright red blood for 2 weeks at age 45 without pain or bowel-change suggests a distal anorectal source (hemorrhoid/anal fissure) but we still must rule out rectal cancer or inflammatory causes. 2) Do you notice a tender “lump” at the anus (worse with wiping/sitting) versus a firm mass deeper in the rectum that persists?
Patient: I don’t feel a tender lump at the anus, and nothing seems worse with wiping or sitting—no mass that persists deeper either. I’ve only noticed the bright red bleeding with bowel movements.

Doctor: Thanks—no tender perianal lump makes an anal fissure less likely; with 45-year-old new bright red bleeding for 2 weeks and a “palpable rectal mass,” we must evaluate for a distal rectal tumor. REQUEST TEST: Rectal_exam_with_proctoscopy (or rigid sigmoidoscopy) Doctor: Also, REQUEST TEST: CBC (for anemia) and Iron_studies (if iron deficiency), and if a lesion is seen, we’ll need biopsy. Doctor: Can you confirm—when you say “palpable rectal mass,” did you feel it yourself, or did I find it on my exam (if you’ve had one)? And do you have any family history of colorectal cancer/polyps or inflammatory bowel disease?

RESULTS: - Vital Signs: Temperature 36.7°C (98.1°F); Blood Pressure 115/85 mmHg; Heart Rate 72 bpm; Respiratory Rate 15 breaths/min. - Rectovaginal/Rectal Exam: Palpable, non-tender, prolapsed mass that can be easily pushed back into the anal sphincter by the examiner’s finger. - CBC: WBC normal; Hemoglobin within normal limits; Platelets within normal limits. - Anoscopy/Proctoscopy Findings: Visualization of internal hemorrhoids. - Note: No iron studies provided. No biopsy results provided.

Doctor: A prolapsed, easily reducible non-tender mass with anoscopy showing internal hemorrhoids fits internal hemorrhoid bleeding causing the palpable/prolapsed finding; since CBC is normal there’s no current anemia, which is reassuring. Can you tell me whether you’re straining or constipated, and if you’ve had any black/tarry stools or bleeding since today? DIAGNOSIS READY: Internal hemorrhoids with reducible prolapsed internal hemorrhoid causing bright red rectal bleeding (no anemia; low suspicion for malignancy given exam/proctoscopy findings).
